claim: Heuer defines diagnosticity: evidence that fits every hypothesis has little or no value for choosing between them.
quote: If an item of evidence seems consistent with all the hypotheses, it may have no diagnostic value at all.
title: Psychology of Intelligence Analysis
venue: CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence
transfer: Program drops evidence items marked consistent with all rival hypotheses before any scoring.

claim: Heuer's ACH step 5 says to try to disprove hypotheses rather than prove them, following the scientific method.
quote: Proceed by trying to disprove hypotheses rather than prove them.
title: Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 8
venue: CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence
transfer: Count inconsistencies per hypothesis in code, pick fewest; used only at a split among attempts.

claim: Heuer warns against rejecting an unproven hypothesis as if it were disproved, because early rejection stops the search for supporting evidence.
quote: Early rejection of unproven, but not disproved, hypotheses biases the subsequent analysis, because one does not then look for the evidence that might support them.
title: Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 8
venue: CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence
transfer: Keep a 'live but unproven' tag on rival answers; only discard on a positive contradiction, not on absence of support.

claim: Heuer reports a medical-diagnosis study: doctors who stressed thorough data collection were less accurate than those who identified and tested hypotheses, and extra data did not raise accuracy.
quote: Those who stressed thorough collection of data as their principal analytical method were significantly less accurate in their diagnoses than those who described themselves as following other analytical strategies
authors: Richards J. Heuer Jr. (citing physician-diagnosis research)
title: Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 4
venue: CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence
transfer: Prefer hypothesis-testing steps over a 'gather more context' step; do not add retrieval rounds by default. Secondary citation, original not read.

claim: Heuer describes Wason's 2-4-6 task as evidence that people seek confirming rather than disconfirming tests, the same bias later measured in LLMs.
quote: One can only disprove the hypothesis by citing an ascending sequence of odd numbers and learning that this, too, conforms to the rule.
title: Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 4
venue: CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence
transfer: When testing a hypothesis, program asks for a test whose failure would refute it, not one that fits it.

claim: Heuer advises a sensitivity check on linchpin assumptions: ask what could make each assumption out of date.
quote: Those linchpin assumptions that drive the analysis are the ones that need to be questioned.
title: Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 5
venue: CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence
transfer: Key assumptions check at an impasse: list assumptions behind the leading answer, negate the unverified ones, run one attempt each.

claim: In a randomized trial of 50 UK intelligence analysts, ACH did not improve accuracy; the control group was slightly more accurate.
quote: the control group was a little more accurate (and coherent) than the ACH group
authors: Mandel DR, Karvetski CW, Dhami MK
title: Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
transfer: Do not run a full ACH procedure by default; treat it as a candidate to measure, not a given.

claim: Mean absolute error was 0.26 for ACH versus 0.21 for control in the same trial (control better).
authors: Mandel DR, Karvetski CW, Dhami MK
title: Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
transfer: none (effect size anchor; ACH arm was 0.26 [0.22, 0.29])

claim: Forcing probabilities over exclusive hypotheses to sum to 1 (coherentization) cut error by 35%, and averaging analysts after that cut error by 61%.
quote: decreased by 61% after first coherentizing their judgments
authors: Mandel DR, Karvetski CW, Dhami MK
title: Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
transfer: Any probability vector the agent outputs is normalized in code; average several varied-prompt calls. Same-model samples are correlated, so gain may shrink.

claim: ACH-trained analysts did not complete all ACH steps, results on confirmation bias were mixed, and ACH may increase inconsistency and error.
quote: we observed that ACH may increase judgement inconsistency and error
authors: Dhami MK, Belton IK, Mandel DR
title: The 'analysis of competing hypotheses' in intelligence analysis
transfer: A program never skips steps, so this human failure mode is removed; the inconsistency failure may remain. Measure it.

claim: With 227 online participants, ACH showed no coherence advantage over no technique across several tests.
quote: Across multiple tests of coherence, the ACH group showed no advantage over a no-technique control group.
title: Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help?
transfer: none (null result; supports gating any matrix step)

claim: ACH users were less reliable across matched isomorphic cases (p = .051, small effect d = 0.20), and both groups were very conservative.
quote: Participants who used ACH were less reliable across isomorphic cases than control participants
title: Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help?
transfer: Test an agent's matrix step for run-to-run consistency on paired rephrasings of one case, not only accuracy.

claim: In a further experiment, ACH and a factorized Bayes method did not improve accuracy, ACH lowered coherence, while coherentization and aggregation gave large accuracy gains.
quote: Analytic techniques such as ACH and FBT were ineffective in improving accuracy and handling correlated evidence, and ACH in fact decreased the coherence of probability judgments.
authors: Karvetski CW, Mandel DR, Irwin D
title: Improving Probability Judgment in Intelligence Analysis: From Structured Analysis to Statistical Aggregation
transfer: Prefer post-hoc statistical repair (normalize, aggregate) over adding judged procedure steps.

claim: A critical review of all ACH experiments (7 articles, 6 experiments) concludes ACH as a whole gives little to no benefit and may reduce judgment quality; some components may help. Preprint.
quote: ACH—as a whole—has little to no overall benefit on judgment quality
title: Critical review of the Analysis of Competing Hypotheses technique: Lessons for the intelligence community
transfer: Keep only the parts with a separate rationale (drop non-diagnostic evidence, test the rival), not the whole ACH ritual.

claim: Hypotheses in rows with evidence in columns reduced confirmation bias (N=161); the standard ACH matrix (hypotheses in columns) and text did not; 62 Dutch military analysts mostly showed no confirmation bias.
quote: individuals presented with hypotheses in rows and evidence items in columns were significantly less likely to demonstrate confirmation bias
authors: Dhami MK, Belton IK, De Werd P, Hadzhieva V, Wicke L
title: Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
transfer: A/B test table layout (options as rows) in the evidence-weighing prompt. This corrects the earlier brief, which had the layout direction and the analyst result unclear.

claim: The ACH-style matrix gave no benefit for sensitivity to evidence credibility, and coherence or cognitive reflection did not separate better and worse performers.
quote: The ACH-style matrix also did not confer any benefits regarding increasing sensitivity to evidence credibility.
authors: Dhami MK, Belton IK, De Werd P, Hadzhieva V, Wicke L
title: Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
transfer: Source reliability must be scored by its own step; the matrix does not do it.

claim: An online experiment (N=159) found ACH did not reduce adversarial allegiance or change credibility ratings in mock expert witnesses.
quote: the ACH method may have limited utility as a debiasing strategy
title: The analysis of competing hypotheses and expert witness testimony: Counteracting adversarial allegiance in witness credibility assessments?
transfer: none (another null; the bias came from the assigned side, so an agent given a side should be re-run from a neutral frame)

claim: Analysts' tradecraft norms are only loosely grounded in judgment science, were never validity-tested, and may reduce rather than raise quality; warnings against one bias can cause its mirror-image bias.
quote: the prevailing tradecraft norms of best practice are only loosely grounded in the science of judgment and decision-making.
title: Correcting Judgment Correctives in National Security Intelligence
transfer: Always-doubt prompts can overshoot into underconfidence; check both error directions, as our NoveltyBench vs puzzle results show.

claim: Mandel and Barnes scored 1,514 real strategic intelligence forecasts: discrimination and calibration were very good, and the main error was underconfidence; recalibration reduced it.
quote: Miscalibration was mainly due to underconfidence such that analysts assigned more uncertainty than needed
title: Accuracy of forecasts in strategic intelligence
transfer: Fit a recalibration map on the agent's own stated confidence vs outcomes; apply it in code. Observational field data, not a trial.

claim: Brief instruction in information structuring made 43 analysts' probability judgments more coherent (more additive, more Bayes-compliant).
quote: After instruction, analysts' probability judgments were more coherent (i.e., more additive and compliant with Bayes theorem).
title: Instruction in information structuring improves Bayesian judgment in intelligence analysts
transfer: Pre/post design without control group; supports a nested-frequency or natural-frequency restatement step for probability questions.

claim: In a geopolitical forecasting tournament, probability training, teaming and tracking improved calibration and resolution; training taught reference classes and averaging.
quote: Probability training corrected cognitive biases, encouraged forecasters to use reference classes, and provided forecasters with heuristics, such as averaging when multiple estimates were available.
authors: Mellers B, Ungar L, Baron J, et al.
title: Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
transfer: Add a reference-class step (what fraction of similar cases) and average several calls for forecast-type questions.

claim: Mandel and Irwin argue the structured-analytic-technique approach has serious conceptual problems and little research support, and propose statistical post-analysis methods instead. Preprint.
quote: The SAT approach, however, suffers from serious conceptual problems and a paucity of support from scientific research.
title: Beyond Bias Minimization: Improving Intelligence with Statistical Optimization and Human Augmentation
transfer: Build repair-by-statistics (recalibrate, weight calls by past accuracy) before procedure steps.

claim: A book of ACH experiments by Whitesmith critiques ACH as lacking a sound theoretical or empirical basis and includes meta-analyses of confirmation bias and serial-position effects.
quote: Critiques the CIA's Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (ACH) method, argues it lacks a sound theoretical or empirical basis
title: Cognitive Bias in Intelligence Analysis: Testing the Analysis of Competing Hypotheses Method
transfer: none yet (publisher record via Crossref only; chapters not read). Whitesmith's conclusion that early focal hypotheses drive confirmation bias suggests listing rivals before commitment.

claim: Across eleven LLMs on a Wason 2-4-6 style task, models often chose confirming rather than testing triples; counterexample prompting raised rule discovery from 42% to 56%, and distillation transferred to the Blicket test.
quote: confirmation bias is a limitation of LLMs in hypothesis exploration.
authors: Jhaveri AR, GX-Chen A, Sucholutsky I, Choi E
title: Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
transfer: In hidden-rule tasks with feedback, force each test to be one whose failure refutes the leading hypothesis.

claim: AgentCDM, an LLM multi-agent framework inspired by ACH, reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks, with no numbers or baseline names given in the abstract.
quote: Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that AgentCDM achieves state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Zhao X, Zhao S, Yu H, Zhang L, Li Q
title: AgentCDM: Enhancing Multi-Agent Collaborative Decision-Making via ACH-Inspired Structured Reasoning
transfer: Weak signal only: the one LLM paper using ACH reports gains but with trained scaffolding; read the full text before relying on it.

claim: Schwenk's 1990 meta-analysis of devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry exists, but its abstract and effect sizes could not be opened.
quote: No abstract is available for this item.
title: Effects of devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry on decision making: A meta-analysis
venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 47(1), 161-176
transfer: none until effect sizes are read; the earlier brief's claim rests on search summaries only
